system: Jewish sha'ot zemaniyot (שעות זמניות, "seasonal" or "proportional" hours) — the halachic division of the daytime span into twelve equal parts, so that an hour lengthens in summer and shortens in winter, and every rabbinically fixed time of day (latest Shema, latest morning prayer, chatzot, mincha gedola, mincha ketana, plag ha-mincha) is stated as a count of them. Rema names the unit in his gloss to Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 233:1 (S7-a). This dossier's subject is narrower than the hours themselves: it is the set of opinions that CHANGE THE CLOCK — where the twelve-fold span starts and ends (Magen Avraham vs. the Vilna Gaon), whether the dawn and dusk intervals are measured in fixed minutes or in solar depression angles, and whether "sunrise" names the sea-level geometric event, an elevation-adjusted one, or the visibly observed one. This is current religious practice for millions of people, computed daily by printed luchot, synagogue boards and phone apps; it is not a historical curiosity, and it carries no claim of predictive or operative validity of any kind.

dayStart:
THE START OF THE TWELVE-FOLD SPAN IS THE DISPUTE, NOT A SETTLED VALUE. That is the single most important fact about this system, and an engine must carry the opinion as a parameter rather than pick a default.

Both positions stand in one sentence of the Mishnah Berurah at OC 58:4: ומונין אלו הג' שעות מזמן עמוד השחר כן כתב המ"א ודעת הגר"א משעת הנץ החמה — we count these three hours from amud ha-shachar, so wrote the Magen Avraham; and the opinion of the Gra is from the time of ha-netz ha-chamah (S11-a; Warsaw 1884–1907, term expired, public domain in the United States).

(a) MAGEN AVRAHAM — alot ha-shachar to tzeit ha-kochavim. The Magen Avraham's own words at OC 58:1: נ"ל דהכא לכ"ע מנינן מעלות השחר — it appears to me that here, by all opinions, we count from alot ha-shachar (S10-a; first published Dyhernfurth 1692, digitised from a 19th-century NLI imprint, term expired, public domain in the United States). Mishnah Berurah 443:8 sets the two schemes side by side and assigns this one to many Acharonim: וחושבין את היום מעלות השחר עד צאת הכוכבים כ"כ הרבה אחרונים וי"א דחושבין מהנץ החמה עד עת השקיעה (S12-a). The scheme is older than the Magen Avraham: Terumat ha-Deshen I:1, mid-15th century, already computes plag ha-mincha on a summer day of some eighteen hours מעלות השחר עד צאת הכוכבים (S16-a; Warsaw 1882, term expired, PD-US). The Zemaneh Yosef implementers name the Terumat ha-Deshen alongside the Magen Avraham for exactly this reason (S25-b, paraphrased, in copyright). Touger's footnote to Hilchot Kriat Shema 1:11 and Gewirtz's Ḥakirah article state it in English (S5-a, S19-b; both cite-only, paraphrased).

(b) VILNA GAON — ha-netz ha-chamah to shki'at ha-chamah. Mishnah Berurah 443:8 continues, immediately after S12-a: ודעת הגר"א כמותם ולכתחלה טוב להחמיר כדעה א' — the Gra's opinion is like theirs, and lechatchila it is good to be stringent per the first view (S12-b). Shulchan Aruch HaRav OC 443:4 states the sunrise-to-sunset day explicitly (S17-a; Kehot vocalized edition is CC-BY-NC, paraphrased here, not quoted). Gewirtz states it as one of the two fundamental areas in zemanim (S19-a), and the Zemaneh Yosef FAQ states it as the practical rule (S25-a); both paraphrased.

FIRST CONFLICT, KEPT. The Shulchan Aruch HaRav defines the day as netz-to-shki'ah at OC 443:4 (S17-a) and counts the three hours of Shema from alot ha-shachar at OC 58:3 (S17-c); Touger's footnote places the Shulchan Aruch HaRav with the Vilna Gaon (S5-b). Three snippets, two of them from the same author. This dossier does not pick.

SECOND CONFLICT, KEPT. "Alot to tzeit" is not one arithmetic. Gewirtz records that the evening endpoint of the Magen Avraham calculation, which falls after sunset, is itself in dispute (S19-c, paraphrased). Any implementation offering a single column labelled MGA is offering a family of arithmetics under one label.

THIRD THING, AND IT IS AN ARITHMETIC TRAP FOR AN IMPLEMENTER. Gewirtz reports the practical paradox that computing sha'ot zemaniyot on the Magen Avraham's opinion requires first computing with the Gaon's endpoints, because the dawn and dusk offsets are themselves defined relative to sunrise and sunset (S26-d, paraphrased).

WHAT THIS LEDGER DOES NOT ESTABLISH. The rollover of the halachic CALENDAR day — the evening boundary at which the date, Shabbat and festivals change — is a different question from the start of the twelve-fold daytime span, and no snippet in this ledger addresses it. It is recorded in gaps[] rather than supplied from memory.
divisionRule:
TWELVE, ALWAYS, WHATEVER THE DAY'S LENGTH. Nothing is rounded to sixty minutes.

The naming statement is Rema's gloss to Shulchan Arukh OC 233:1: ומשערינן שעות אלו לפי ענין היום ואף אם היום ארוך משערינן לי"ב שעות והם נקראים שעות זמניות — we measure these hours according to the character of the day, and even if the day is long we measure it as twelve hours, and these are called sha'ot zemaniyot (S7-a; Maginei Eretz, Lemberg 1893, term expired, public domain in the United States). The fetcher records that Rema there cites Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Berakhot ch. 1; that Commentary was not retrieved and is not relied on here.

The same rule independently, and two centuries earlier: Terumat ha-Deshen I:1 quotes a responsum received from one of the great ones — לחשוב היום לעולם רק לי"ב שעות אפי' לימים ארוכים לענין פלג המנחה (S16-b; Warsaw 1882, term expired, PD-US) — rendered by Sefaria's CC0 community translation as "daylight should always be split into twelve, even in the long summer days, in order to calculate Plag Hamincha" (S16-c; CC0, quotable). Shulchan Aruch HaRav OC 58:3 gives the definitional sentence, that these hours are zemaniyot since every day, long or short, is divided into twelve (S17-b; Kehot, CC-BY-NC, paraphrased). Touger's footnote glosses them as one-twelfth of the duration of the daylight hours (S5-c; CC-BY-NC, paraphrased).

THE ARITHMETIC, WHICH IS NOT ITSELF IN DISPUTE IN THIS LEDGER:
    shaah zemanit = (END − START) / 12
    boundary(n)   = START + n × shaah zemanit,  n = 1…12
START and END are supplied by the chosen opinion (see variants[]). Every disagreement recorded in this dossier is a disagreement about START and END, or about how to locate them, never about the division into twelve.

THE FRACTIONS THE SOURCES THEMSELVES STATE. Shulchan Arukh OC 58:1 calls the end of the third hour רביע היום, a quarter of the day (S6-a; CC0 English at S6-b). Rambam, Hilchot Tefillah 3:1, calls the end of the fourth hour שלישית היום, a third of the day (S4-a; Torat Emet digitisation declared public domain, underlying work 12th century, term expired). Those two fractions are the internal check that the division is proportional and not clock-based: 3/12 and 4/12.

THE NIGHT — THIS LEDGER IS THIN HERE AND SAYS SO. The only snippet that divides the night is the 1901–06 Jewish Encyclopedia's gloss on the term, describing "periodical hours, whose length is equal to one-twelfth of either the day or the night, whichever is the longer" (S23-g; published 1901–1906, term expired, public domain in the United States), which attributes the usage to Maimonides. That wording is the article's own and is odd on its face. No Tier A snippet in this ledger states the twelve-fold division of the night. A night column must not be built on S23-g alone; see gaps[].
rulerColumnJustification:
FALSE — and the search that establishes it is in the ledger rather than asserted, because a fabricated confirmed gap is worse than a missing row.

No snippet retrieved assigns a planetary or any other ruler to a sha'ah zemanit. A seven-planet hour rotation DOES exist in rabbinic literature over the same twelve-hour daytime division. Bavli Shabbat 129b, in the bloodletting sugya, asks why one does not let blood on Tuesday and answers that Mars stands at the even hours; the hour-ruler premise is assumed there rather than spelled out (S18-a; the only digitisation retrieved is the William Davidson edition, CC-BY-NC, so this is paraphrased and not reproduced). Rashi supplies the rotation in full, and the Vilna Shas digitisation of Rashi is public domain (printed 1880–1886, term expired):
    שעה ראשונה של ד' בשבת שימש שבתאי ובשניה צדק ואחריו מאדים ואחריו חמה ואחריו נוגה ואחריו כוכב ואחריו לבנה (S18-b)
    נמצאו ז' המזלות לז' השעות וחוזרים חלילה לעולם (S18-c)
    נמצא מאדים חוזר בו חלילה בשעה שמינית ביום והיא זוגות (S18-d)
That is the Saturn–Jupiter–Mars–Sun–Venus–Mercury–Moon rotation, cycling perpetually, explicitly indexed to numbered hours of the daytime.

It is not a ruler column and must not be used as one. It appears in an astrological/medical sugya about when to let blood, and nothing in this ledger applies it to the halachic prayer clock or names the ruler of a sha'ah zemanit. Per the maintainer's grid ruling of 2026-08-01 — the comparison is asymmetric and the absence is taught — zmanim renders NO ruler column. L21/L22 are the evidence that the question was asked; the corresponding gaps[] entry records the search. Every entry below omits the ruler property entirely rather than writing "none" or "unattested" into it, because a renderer reads the field and a filled field is a claim.

entries.name: First seasonal hour of the day
entries.quality: ITS START IS THE START OF THE WHOLE SPAN, and which solar event that is, is the system's central dispute — so this boundary is a pair of times, not one. Magen Avraham OC 58:1 counts from alot ha-shachar (S10-a); the Gra counts from ha-netz ha-chamah as reported by Mishnah Berurah 58:4 (S11-a) and 443:8 (S12-a, S12-b). Rambam, Hilchot Tefillah 3:1, gives the morning prayer's mitzvah as beginning with ha-netz ha-chamah — תפלת השחר מצותה שיתחיל להתפלל עם הנץ החמה (S4-a).
entries.note: A second, finer question sits underneath the word "sunrise" itself. Magen Avraham OC 58:2 reads the Beit Yosef as implying that from when the sun begins to shine until its body has risen is an hour, and records a variant reading of a tenth of an hour: משמע בב"י משיתחיל לזרוח עד שיעלה גוף השמש הוא שעה ויש גורסין כמו עישור שעה אחת (S10-b). Rambam's vatikin interval at Hilchot Kriat Shema 1:11 carries the same variant in the digitisation's own square brackets — ושעור זה כמו [עשור] שעה קדם שתעלה השמש (S4-c). Both are quotable: Lemberg-era Magen Avraham and the Torat Emet Rambam are declared public domain.

entries.name: Third seasonal hour of the day
entries.quality: ITS END IS SOF ZMAN KRIAT SHEMA, the latest time for the morning Shema. Shulchan Arukh OC 58:1: ונמשך זמנה עד סוף ג' שעות שהוא רביע היום — it continues until the end of three hours, which is a quarter of the day (S6-a; Lemberg 1893, term expired, PD-US; Sefaria's CC0 English at S6-b). WHICH clock those three hours run on is the dispute this dossier exists to record: from alot ha-shachar per Magen Avraham OC 58:1 (S10-a), from ha-netz ha-chamah per the Gra as reported by Mishnah Berurah 58:4 (S11-a). This boundary is therefore two times on the same morning, and the gap between them is the widest practical consequence of the whole disagreement.
entries.note: Rambam gives the same limit at Hilchot Kriat Shema 1:11 — שעונתה עד סוף שלש שעות ביום — in a clause that concerns one who transgressed and delayed (S4-b; Torat Emet digitisation declared public domain, underlying work 12th century). The Shulchan Aruch HaRav counts these three hours from alot ha-shachar at OC 58:3 (S17-c) while the same author defines the day as netz-to-shki'ah at OC 443:4 (S17-a); Touger's footnote places him with the Vilna Gaon (S5-b). This dossier keeps all three and resolves none of them.

entries.name: Fourth seasonal hour of the day
entries.quality: ITS END IS THE LIMIT OF THE MORNING PRAYER FOR R. YEHUDA, and Rambam rules with him. Mishnah Berakhot 4:1: תפלת השחר, עד חצות. רבי יהודה אומר, עד ארבע שעות — the morning prayer, until chatzot; R. Yehuda says, until four hours (S1-a; Torat Emet Hebrew digitisation declared public domain, the Mishnah itself ancient). Rambam, Hilchot Tefillah 3:1: וזמנה עד סוף שעה רביעית שהיא שלישית היום — its time is until the end of the fourth hour, which is a third of the day (S4-a). The fraction the sources state is 4/12.
entries.note: A TRANSLATION ARTEFACT WORTH RECORDING, because it is exactly the ambiguity this dossier is about. The Hebrew of R. Yehuda's clause at S1-a fixes no anchor: it says four hours and stops. The William Davidson English rendering at S1-c supplies a sunrise anchor that the Hebrew does not carry. That rendering is CC-BY-NC and is therefore paraphrased here rather than reproduced. An implementer reading only the English would take the Gra's endpoints as the Mishnah's own, and the Mishnah does not say so.

entries.name: Sixth seasonal hour of the day
entries.quality: ITS END IS CHATZOT, the midpoint of the span and the first tanna's limit for the morning prayer: תפלת השחר, עד חצות (S1-a). Because chatzot here is 6/12 of the daytime span, it moves with the chosen endpoints exactly as every other boundary does; on the Magen Avraham's alot-to-tzeit span it is not the same instant as on the Gra's netz-to-shki'ah span.
entries.note: The name is the Mishnah's own word and is quoted from the Torat Emet Hebrew digitisation, declared public domain. This ledger carries no snippet identifying chatzot with solar transit or true local noon; that identification is a common one in the practical literature and it is recorded in gaps[] rather than asserted here.

entries.name: Seventh seasonal hour of the day
entries.quality: MINCHA GEDOLA FALLS INSIDE THIS HOUR, AT ITS MIDPOINT — at six and a half hours, not at a boundary of the hour. Shulchan Arukh OC 233:1: מי שהתפלל תפלת המנחה לאחר שש שעות ומחצה ולמעלה יצא — one who prayed mincha from six and a half hours onward has fulfilled the obligation (S7-b; Lemberg 1893, term expired, PD-US). The label "mincha gedola" does not appear in the retrieved Hebrew and is not put in nameOriginal.

entries.name: Tenth seasonal hour of the day
entries.quality: MINCHA KETANA FALLS INSIDE THIS HOUR, AT ITS MIDPOINT — the principal time of the afternoon prayer, from nine and a half hours until night: ועיקר זמנה מט' שעות ומחצה ולמעלה עד הלילה (S7-b). entries.note: The se'if's phrase עד הלילה — until night — hands the end of this window to the nightfall question, which is where the ledger's densest disagreement sits: see variants[] on bein ha-shmashot and tzeit ha-kochavim, and contestedPoints[].

entries.name: Eleventh seasonal hour of the day
entries.quality: PLAG HA-MINCHA FALLS THREE-QUARTERS OF THE WAY THROUGH THIS HOUR — at ten and three-quarter elapsed hours. Shulchan Arukh OC 233:1: ולרבי יהודה עד פלג המנחה שהוא עד סוף י"א שעות חסר רביע — and for R. Yehuda, until plag ha-mincha, which is until the end of eleven hours less a quarter (S7-c). Mishnah Berakhot 4:1 is the root: תפלת המנחה עד הערב. רבי יהודה אומר, עד פלג המנחה (S1-b).
entries.note: Plag is the boundary that forced the twelve-fold rule into the open. Terumat ha-Deshen I:1 reaches it by asking what to do when the day runs to some eighteen hours from alot ha-shachar to tzeit ha-kochavim in some lands at the height of summer (S16-a), and answers with the responsum that the day is always reckoned as twelve hours even on long days (S16-b, CC0 English at S16-c). The naming statement in Rema OC 233:1 (S7-a) sits in the same siman for the same reason.

entries.name: Twelfth seasonal hour of the day
entries.quality: ITS END IS THE END OF THE WHOLE SPAN, and like the start it is a pair of times rather than one. On the Gra's scheme it is shki'at ha-chamah (S12-a, S17-a, S19-a, S25-a); on the Magen Avraham's it is tzeit ha-kochavim (S12-a, S5-a, S25-b) — and Gewirtz records that this evening endpoint is itself in dispute even within the Magen Avraham's scheme (S19-c), so "tzeit" here names a family of values and not one. Mishnah Berakhot 4:1 gives the plain limit of the afternoon prayer as עד הערב, until evening (S1-b).
entries.note: Everything the ledger holds about how this endpoint is located — the four-mil and five-mil intervals, the 18-, 22.5- and 24-minute mil, the 8.5° and 4.37° tzeit, the three-quarter-mil bein ha-shmashot, and the two-sunsets scheme reported in the name of Rabbeinu Tam — is set out in variants[] under the axes "dusk-interval" and "nightfall", each with its own snippet ids. It is deliberately not summarised into a single value here.

variants.label: Vilna Gaon: ha-netz ha-chamah to shki'at ha-chamah (sunrise to sunset)
variants.authority: The Vilna Gaon, as reported by Mishnah Berurah 443:8 (S12-b) and 58:4 (S11-a). Shulchan Aruch HaRav OC 443:4 states the same arithmetic in its own voice (S17-a). Touger's footnote to Hilchot Kriat Shema 1:11 groups the Shulchan Aruch HaRav with the Vilna Gaon (S5-b). Gewirtz (S19-a) and the Zemaneh Yosef implementers (S25-a) state it in English. NOTE ON PROVENANCE: the Gaon's own words for THIS proposition are not in this ledger — S14-a/b/c are his words on bein ha-shmashot at Beur HaGra OC 261:2, not on the endpoints of the twelve-fold span. Every attribution of the endpoints to the Gra here is a report of him.
variants.arithmetic: START = ha-netz ha-chamah (sunrise). END = shki'at ha-chamah (sunset). shaah = (sunset − sunrise) / 12. boundary(n) = sunrise + n × shaah. This is the column printed as GRA in luchot and implemented as the default seasonal hour in zmanim libraries.

variants.label: Magen Avraham: alot ha-shachar to tzeit ha-kochavim (dawn to nightfall)
variants.authority: Magen Avraham OC 58:1 in his own words (S10-a). Mishnah Berurah 58:4 (S11-a) and 443:8, which assigns the scheme to many Acharonim (S12-a). Terumat ha-Deshen I:1 uses the same alot-to-tzeit day in the mid-15th century (S16-a), and the Zemaneh Yosef FAQ names the Terumat ha-Deshen alongside the Magen Avraham (S25-b). Touger (S5-a) and Gewirtz (S19-b) state it in English.
variants.arithmetic: START = alot ha-shachar. END = tzeit ha-kochavim. shaah = (tzeit − alot) / 12. boundary(n) = alot + n × shaah. THE ARITHMETIC IS NOT CLOSED BY THIS: neither alot nor tzeit is a single value — see the dawn-interval, dusk-interval and fixed-vs-degrees axes below, each of which yields a different MGA column.
variants.keepBoth: Gewirtz records that the evening endpoint of the Magen Avraham calculation is itself in dispute (S19-c). "MGA" is a family of arithmetics, not one.
variants.caveat: Gewirtz also reports that computing on this opinion requires first computing with the Gaon's endpoints, because the dawn and dusk offsets are defined relative to sunrise and sunset (S26-d).

variants.label: Four mil at an 18-minute mil = 72 fixed minutes
variants.authority: Bavli Pesachim 94a, the baraita of R. Yehuda putting four mil between alot ha-shachar and ha-netz ha-chamah, and four between shki'ah and tzeit ha-kochavim (S2-b, S2-c; William Davidson edition, CC-BY-NC, paraphrased here, not reproduced). The mil is fixed at Shulchan Arukh OC 459:2: ושיעור מיל הוי רביעית שעה וחלק מעשרים מן השעה — a quarter of an hour and a twentieth of an hour (S8-a; Lemberg 1893, term expired, PD-US; Sefaria CC0 English at S8-b). The Jewish Encyclopedia derives the same 18 minutes from a 40-mil day of twelve hours and states R. Judah's figure as 4 mils = 72 minutes (S23-a, S23-d; 1901–1906, term expired, PD-US). Peninei Halakhah gives 72 minutes as the first of two practical schemes (S22-d2, paraphrased). The Jewish Action review points to the Chazon Ish OC 13 for the 40-mil-day view that justifies the 18-minute mil (S24-e, paraphrased; second-hand, and the Chazon Ish itself was not retrieved).
variants.arithmetic: ¼ hour + 1/20 hour = 15 + 3 = 18 minutes per mil. 4 mil × 18 = 72 minutes. alot = sunrise − 72 min; tzeit = sunset + 72 min. Arithmetic reproducible from S8-a alone.
variants.caveat: The fetcher records that the four-mil baraita at Pesachim 94a is immediately followed by the sugya's concluding refutation formula, and locates it there (S2-d; William Davidson edition, CC-BY-NC, so it is cited and not reproduced). What that refutation bears on is not established by this ledger and is not asserted here.

variants.label: Ninety fixed minutes — reached by two different routes, and this dossier keeps both
variants.authority: ROUTE 1, five mil at 18 minutes: Bavli Pesachim 94a, R. Yohanan reported by Rabba bar bar Hana, five mil from alot to netz (S2-a, paraphrased); the Jewish Encyclopedia states the full dawn period per R. Johanan as 5 mils, or 90 minutes (S23-c, PD-US). ROUTE 2, four mil at a 22.5-minute mil: Peninei Halakhah, footnote 1, gives ninety minutes on a 22.5-minute mil and observes that this is what is printed in many calendars (S22-d3, paraphrased).

The two routes agree on the minute count and disagree on the mil, so they diverge immediately on every other quantity derived from a mil — including bein ha-shmashot at ¾ mil, which is 13.5 minutes on route 1 and 16.875 on route 2 (see the nightfall axis).
variants.keepBoth: Both derivations are attested and they are not the same claim. Merging them into "90 minutes" loses the mil, which is the parameter everything else is built on.

variants.caveat: THE GRA'S OWN POSITION ON MIL-LENGTH IS NOT IN THIS LEDGER. The locus usually cited for it, Beur HaGra OC 459:2, was retrieved and contains a short remark about flour and kneading. See gaps[] — and see honestLimits, because this contradicts a claim in the phase-1 report and the contradiction is left open rather than resolved by the compiler.

variants.label: The degree method: the fixed minute counts hold only for one place and one season
variants.authority: Mishnah Berurah 261:23 states the halachic warrant inside the classical literature: דלכ"ע השעור דג' רבעי מיל משתנה לפי הזמן והמקום ולא נאמר זה בגמרא אלא באופק בבל ובזמן ניסן ותשרי — by all opinions the measure changes with time and place, and was said in the Gemara only for the horizon of Bavel in Nisan and Tishrei (S13-b; Warsaw 1884–1907, term expired, PD-US). Beur HaGra OC 261:2 says the same of bein ha-shmashot: באופק בבל ובזמן תקופת ניסן ותשרי (S14-c; Lemberg 1893, PD-US). MyZmanim states that alos cannot be defined as a fixed amount of time before sunrise, attributing the ruling to the Gra and others, and that 72 minutes applies only to equinox days in Bavel and Eretz Yisrael (S21-d, S21-a, paraphrased). variants.arithmetic: Replace "sunrise − 72 min" with "the moment the sun's centre is D degrees below the horizon", solved per date and latitude. Gewirtz defines a depression angle as a measure of how far below the horizon the sun appears to have descended (S19-f, paraphrased).
variants.caveat: The classical sources cited here (S13-b, S14-c, S15-d) establish that the measure varies with place and season. They do not state a degree figure; every degree figure in this ledger comes from a Tier C practitioner or software source.

variants.label: Bein ha-shmashot at three-quarters of a mil
variants.authority: Bavli Shabbat 34b: the amoraic measure reported by Rabba in the name of Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, which the sugya resolves as three quarters of a mil (S3-c, paraphrased; Davidson edition, CC-BY-NC). polarBehaviour:
WHAT THE LEDGER SAYS, AND NOTHING COMPUTED HERE. Round 1 published nine derived cut-off latitudes; not one of them is in this ledger and not one is carried forward. No latitude threshold in this dossier was calculated by the compiler.

THE GAON STATES THE FAILURE IN HIS OWN WORDS. Beur HaGra OC 261:2: ובמדינות הנוטין לצפון שע"ה מתחיל בקיץ בחצי הלילה — in the lands inclining northward, alot ha-shachar begins in summer at midnight (S14-b; Lemberg 1893, term expired, public domain in the United States). The same comment carries his observational objection, that the senses refute the long-dawn reckoning for anyone who looks, since dawn is a far greater interval than the interval from sunset to nightfall (S14-a).

THE CLASSICAL WARRANT FOR A VARIABLE CLOCK. Mishnah Berurah 261:23: by all opinions the ¾-mil measure changes with time and place and was stated in the Gemara only for the horizon of Bavel in Nisan and Tishrei (S13-b). Beur HaGra says the same of bein ha-shmashot (S14-c). The Biur Halacha reports the Gra that the Gemara's measure was for Bavel or Eretz Yisrael and lengthens in more northerly lands (S15-d).

THE ONLY EXPLICIT LATITUDES IN THE LEDGER are the Jewish Encyclopedia's: beyond latitude 50°, between June 9 and July 9, and beyond 60°, between April 20 and August 18, dawn and twilight overlap each other (S23-h; 1901–1906, term expired, PD-US).

MAGNITUDE, NOT THRESHOLD. Gewirtz gives the 8.5° interval growing about 16% across the season in Israel (36 to 42 minutes) against about 43% in Prague (48 to 69) (S26-a); holds elevation to be only a rounding error next to latitude, discussing the Amsterdam 48-versus-72-minute problem (S19-e); and records that explicit mention of latitude and its effect on twilight length does not appear in rabbinic literature until the 17th century (S19-h). Peninei Halakhah records that even within Israel, Tzfat's dawn interval runs about a minute and a half longer than Jerusalem's (S22-g). All in copyright; all paraphrased.

COMPILER'S NOTE, FLAGGED AS ARITHMETIC AND NOT AS A SOURCED CLAIM: a deeper depression angle becomes unreachable at a lower latitude than a shallower one, so the degree-based opinions fail before ordinary sunrise does — a 19.8° alot is lost while the sun is still rising. This ledger gives no latitude at which any particular angle fails, and this dossier supplies none. Anyone who needs those numbers must derive them and label them as derived.
contestedPoints: THE ENDPOINTS OF THE TWELVE-FOLD SPAN. Magen Avraham OC 58:1 counts from alot ha-shachar (S10-a); the Gra counts from ha-netz ha-chamah, per Mishnah Berurah 58:4 (S11-a) and 443:8 (S12-a, S12-b). Mishnah Berurah 443:8 also rules that lechatchila one should be stringent per the alot-to-tzeit view (S12-b) — which is a practical ruling, not a resolution of the arithmetic. Both columns stand.

THE SHULCHAN ARUCH HARAV CONTRADICTS ITSELF ACROSS TWO SIMANIM, AND A THIRD SOURCE READS HIM A FOURTH WAY. OC 443:4 defines the day as netz-to-shki'ah (S17-a); OC 58:3 counts the three hours of Shema from alot ha-shachar (S17-c); Touger's footnote groups the Shulchan Aruch HaRav with the Vilna Gaon (S5-b). Recorded, not reconciled — this is the fetcher's flagged live conflict and it is preserved intact.

THE MAGEN AVRAHAM'S EVENING ENDPOINT IS ITSELF IN DISPUTE. Gewirtz states it plainly in a footnote (S19-c). "Alot to tzeit" therefore names a family of arithmetics, and any single MGA column silently picks one member of it.

THE LENGTH OF A MIL: 18 minutes (S8-a, S23-a), 22.5 (S22-d, S22-d3, S24-c) or 24 (recorded by the fetcher as the continuation of the sentence at S22-d, attributed there to a further view). Everything downstream — 72/90/96-minute dawns, 13.5/16.875-minute bein ha-shmashot, 8.5°/4.37° tzeit — forks here.
NINETY MINUTES IS REACHED TWO WAYS AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME CLAIM: five mil at 18 minutes (S2-a, S23-c) and four mil at 22.5 (S22-d3). Agreeing on the product hides a disagreement about the unit.
19.8° (S20-c) AGAINST 19.75° (S22-f) for the same 90-minute dawn at the same place and season. Two published figures, both attested, not averaged.

BEIN HA-SHMASHOT HAS FOUR DEFINITIONS IN ONE TALMUDIC PASSAGE — the reddening east (S3-a), half a mil (S3-b), three quarters of a mil (S3-c), and R. Yosei's position that it has no measurable duration at all but is like the blink of an eye (S3-d) — and three published minute-values downstream: 13½ (S23-b), a variant 12 (S23-b), and Mishnah Berurah's gloss of about a quarter of an hour (S13-a).

WHEN BEIN HA-SHMASHOT BEGINS. The two-sunsets scheme reported in the name of Rabbeinu Tam puts 3¼ mil of full day after the sun's body sets (S15-a, S15-b, S9-b); the Gra holds it begins immediately at shki'ah (S14-c), the Biur Halacha marks him as disagreeing (S15-c), and the Gra adds an observational objection (S14-a). About 72 minutes against about 13½ for the same quantity.

DEGREES AGAINST FIXED MINUTES, AS A LIVE PRESENT-DAY DISPUTE BETWEEN NAMED PEOPLE. Notis argues calendars and apps must use depression angles (S24-a, S24-b) and derives 4.37° for tzeit (S24-c); Hoffman answers that contemporary calendars generally present −8.5° (S24-d). Gewirtz treats fixed intervals as a warning sign (S19-d); MyZmanim says alos cannot be defined as a fixed offset (S21-d).

ELEVATION: THREE POSITIONS PLUS A FOURTH ON OBSTRUCTED HORIZONS, all reported at second hand by KosherJava's javadoc — Bursztyn against elevation for anything but sunrise and sunset (S20-e), Zilber for it (S20-f), Karp for factoring obstructing horizons (S20-i). And two calendars inside one Sephardi tradition disagreeing in practice: elevation included per R. Ovadia Yosef as the implementers report him (S25-c), elevation not used in the Amudeh Horaah calendar (S25-d). Gewirtz meanwhile calls elevation a rounding error next to latitude (S19-e).

THE ENGLISH TRANSLATIONS ADD THINGS THE HEBREW DOES NOT SAY, AND AN IMPLEMENTER WILL INHERIT THEM. The Davidson rendering of Mishnah Berakhot 4:1 supplies a sunrise anchor for R. Yehuda's four hours that the Hebrew at S1-a does not carry (S1-c). Sefaria's CC0 translator appends a bracketed 18-minutes-per-mil gloss at OC 459:2 that is not in the Hebrew (S8-b), and at OC 261:2 appends a metric conversion and an approximate-60-minutes gloss that appear nowhere in the Hebrew of S9-a or S9-b (S9-c). These are the translators' additions, flagged by the fetcher, and they are not treated as data here.

THE MAGEN AVRAHAM HOUR IS IN PRACTICE COMPUTED FROM THE GRA'S ANCHORS. Gewirtz reports the paradox (S26-d): the dawn and dusk offsets that define the MGA span are themselves defined relative to sunrise and sunset. An engine that treats the two opinions as independent will get the dependency wrong.

WHAT THIS DOSSIER IS, AND WHAT IT REFUSES TO BE.

1. NO TIER B EVIDENCE, ON A STRICT READING. The ledger contains no modern secular peer-reviewed source on this arithmetic. The two entries tagged B are Ḥakirah vol. 26 (refereed, but a journal of Jewish law rather than a secular venue) and the 1901–06 Jewish Encyclopedia (signed, scholarly, and 120 years old). Both are carried with their tier caveats attached rather than promoted. The system's evidential weight is Tier A primary and Tier C practitioner literature, with a thin Tier B seam.

2. NO RULER COLUMN, AND THE SEARCH IS ON THE RECORD. hasRulerColumn is false; no entry carries a ruler property at all. Rashi's seven-planet hour rotation at Shabbat 129b (S18-b to S18-d) is real, is indexed to the same numbered daytime hours, and belongs to a bloodletting sugya — it is the evidence that the question was asked, not a column to fill. Per the maintainer's grid ruling the absence is part of the teaching.

3. NO TIMES COMPUTED HERE. Every figure in goldenValues was published by a ledger source. Round 1's Hebcal and Astronomy-Engine times, its derived polar cut-off latitudes, and its 26° row are not carried forward, because no snippet in this ledger supports them. That is a real loss of usable regression data and it is stated as a loss.

4. AN UNRESOLVED CONTRADICTION WITH THIS REPO'S OWN PHASE-1 REPORT. PHASE1-REPORT.md blocker 2 states that Beur HaGra on OC 459:2 sharply rejects the 18-minute reckoning and concludes a 22.5-minute mil, quoting Hebrew for it that has no sid in this ledger and is therefore not reproduced here. This round's fetcher retrieved that ref and found a short comment about flour and kneading. The 22.5-minute mil IS attested in this ledger, but from Peninei Halakhah (S22-d, S22-d3) and the Jewish Action review of Notis (S24-c) — not from the Gra. The compiler cannot adjudicate the retrieval conflict and has not. It is in gaps[] and it needs a human with the Lemberg volume.

5. EVERYTHING IN THE ELEVATION AXIS IS SECOND-HAND. Bursztyn, Zilber, Karp, Benish, the Chazon Ish, Rabbeinu Tam and R. Ovadia Yosef are all present only as someone else reports them. Each is labelled that way in place, and none may be re-attributed directly downstream. The visible-horizon method has no primary source here at all.

6. LICENCE. Verbatim text appears here only from sources verified as PD-US or CC0. The best English available on this subject — the William Davidson Talmud and Mishnah, Touger's Mishneh Torah, Peninei Halakhah, the Kehot Shulchan Aruch HaRav — is CC-BY-NC, which is not one of FRAMING §4.1's four verdicts, so it is cite-only and paraphrased throughout. 7. FOUR EMPTY HOURS, KEPT EMPTY. Hours 2, 5, 8 and 9 carry no halachic landmark from this ledger. Round 1, working from a wider source set, filled some of them. They are left blank here rather than carried across, because a row without a sid is not a row. The blanks are the honest shape of what was retrieved.

8. THIS IS A LIVING PRACTICE AND IS DESCRIBED, NEVER PRESCRIBED. The dossier records what named authorities and named implementations state about the arithmetic of a clock. It makes no efficacy, medical or life-outcome claim of any kind, gives no instruction to any reader, and takes no position on any halachic question. Where sources conflict — and on this subject they conflict at almost every step — both positions are recorded and neither is preferred.
